messages.subject_clean: Dynamic Occupancy Model with Problem Seasons
messages.body_plain:
Aloha,

I have a question about how to handle individual seasons with evidence of lack of fit in a dynamic occupancy model.

I am using the colext function to fit a dynamic occupancy model of pueo (Hawaiian short-eared owl) using eBird observations over a 10 year period. I conducted a MacKenzie Bailey goodness-of-fit test on the global model and found near evidence for lack of fit (p = 0.1) and a highish c-hat (1.83). (note: the GOF is a little preliminary since I ran the initial GOF test with 50 sims to get a general idea and estimate run time with more sims. the 50 sim run took 3.5hrs on 47 cores so it will take ~3 days for 1000 nsim or ~15 days for 5000 nsim)

With the preliminary GOF it appears the model fits the data reasonably well, albeit a bit overdispersed. When looking at the seasonal chi-square tables, however, I see that most seasons appear to fit pretty well, and one season in particular does not fit well (season 6, with 7 and 8 less not too far behind).

Questions:
Is this cause for concern? And if so, what are some ways to improve fit in problem seasons? The col/ext parameters are informed with year and island in the global model.
Would it be appropriate to proceed with model selection using QAIC and the c-hat estimated with 50 sims while the mb.gof.test runs over the next few days, given that the final model is provided the final c-hat when the run finishes?

messages.subject: ZIP / population trends
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am modeling bird trends using N-mixture models. Some key aspects of the data are:  ~ 80 species; ~20 years; fixed distance point counts with 1-4 reps/season; ~2800 sites; lots of NA's in data due to sites being surveyed an average of 5 (of 20) years and number of reps being variable (average of 2). I am trying it in Unmarked with the pcount function.

For the 10 species I've explored so far, ZIP models typically have lower AIC values versus P models. Trend estimates are typically slightly different in magnitude (direction is always the same so far). It's my understanding I can't include covariates on psi (the zero-inflation parameter) in Unmarked. I might ultimately run these models using JAGS, but I have so many species, I feel a little daunted by the amount of time that could take.

I have a few questions:
1) What is the meaning of a psi parameter when there are no covariates on it? Will it function to equally exclude bad sites (where the species isn't) as good sites (where the species is)?
2) Are ZIP models a reasonable thing to consider when the goal is trend estimates? I imagine yes if the data generating process includes a component that's generating zeros unexplained by the component generating counts, but I haven't been able to find precedence for this (in a short search).
3) And, more broadly, are N-mixture models the way to go with these data?

Thank you in advance for any advice and help,

Valerie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Valerie,

Quick responses in italics below.

> 1) What is the meaning of a psi parameter when there are no covariates on it? Will it function to equally exclude bad sites (where the species isn't) as good sites (where the species is)?

Psi is a zero-inflation parameter in this context: the proportion of sites that are (excess) zero's beyond the Poisson part of the model. If the estimate of lambda is large enough that N = 0 | N~P(lambda) is nearly impossible, than this parameter approximates a probability of absence. Otherwise, zeroes can arise as either the zero inflation or the Poisson parts of the model, and I don't know that psi has any clear biological interpretation (maybe somebody else has a good interpretation). I think it would be possible to code something up that gets at whether N = 0 at a given site is arising from the ZI vs. P parts, but I don't think any such function is built-in, and again, not clear to me how to meaningfully interpret this.

> 2) Are ZIP models a reasonable thing to consider when the goal is trend estimates? I imagine yes if the data generating process includes a component that's generating zeros unexplained by the component generating counts, but I haven't been able to find precedence for this (in a short search).

I'm guessing that you are 'stacking' the data for analysis (i.e., year is a covariate in the model, and a 'site' in the unmarked frame really describes some site during a given year). Maybe worth noting that psi is a constant as implemented in unmarked (I think?).  An off-the-top-of head thought is that there is some risk is that the latent zero inflation across 'sites'  (site x year) could easily be more heavily allocated to some years than others. This may not be desirable. Might make more sense to construct a model where the yearly structure is explicit, which might expedite comparison of different formulations, e.g.:
z[i, t]~Bern(psi)
N[i,t] ~ P([1-z[i,t]]*lambda[i,t])
vs.
z[i, t]~Bern(psi[t])
N[i,t] ~ P([1-z[i,t]]*lambda[i,t])
vs.
whatever else--like an open model to capture site-specific dynamics following N[i,t]~P(exp(r)*N[i, t-1]), etc. Doesn't necessarily need to be coded in BUGS fashion.

Cheers,

John

messages.body_plain:
Andrew,

I think the first error related to bootstrapping is a result of issues with optimization. Since you aren't fitting any interaction terms, degree of co-occurrence should not be a major issue. The model apparently converged (after quite a large number of iterations), but occupancy parameter estimates are very imprecise, especially for species 4. This is causing issues with the generation of confidence intervals around predictions. You probably could get predict to work if you set argument se.fit=FALSE, but I would not be very confident in using results from a model with some parameter SEs that are that large. Might be worth trying a different optim algorithm like BFGS or L-BFGS-B, although I suspect you are using Nelder-Mead for a reason.

In your specific case here I'm not sure it makes a lot of sense to fit this as a multi-species model (given my limited info on your situation). You have a pretty small sample size (14 sites) and are trying to handle a relatively large number of species (likely resulting in these poor estimates), but also don't have any species interactions included. I'd at least start by trying to fit single-species occupancy models with covariates for interest for each species, to see if it's even possible in this simpler case. If species 4, for example, is problematic even with a single-species occupancy model then I would consider not attempting to include it in the multispecies model. There may also be better multi-species frameworks to use with your data (see e.g. "Multi‐species occupancy models: review, roadmap, and recommendations", Deverajan et al. 2020).

For the second issue with predicting detection probabilities, I'm not able to replicate that problem myself. If you send me your fitted model saved as an Rdata or Rds I can take a look and see if there's something unique about your model causing issues.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: OccuMulti
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

I think there are some issues with how you constructed your unmarkedFrame. Your object y2k should be a list of matrices, each with #rows = #sites and #cols=#sampling occasions. It looks like you are just creating matrices directly out of data frame columns, which means you only have one column/one replicate sampling occasion per species, which isn't enough info and is likely causing the NaNs in your output. I would suggest taking a close look at the example for occuMulti and specifically what the structure of each part of the y-list looks like to make sure your data match. I think this will also get at your question about having multiple locations - each location should be a row in each of your species matrices and each column a replicate. So if you have 2 species, 10 sites, and 3 replicates per site, you'd end up with a y-list with two elements, each one a 10x3 matrix of 0s and 1s.

Regarding formulas, you can only have 3 state models (species 1, species 2, and species1+2 interaction), but each model can have one or more covariates. So to add more covariates it would look like:

occFormulas <- c('~canopy_cover + elevation + soil', '~soil', '~1')

Then the species 1 formula includes covariates for canopy cover, elevation, and soil, species 2 is just soil, and the interaction has no covariates. I would not suggest just throwing all 8 covariates in to all models right away though. Start simple (as you've done in your example) and build up complexity based on your specific hypotheses for this study.

It's hard to answer the question about unit of replication, since it depends on a lot of factors including the total length of your data collection period and how frequently each species is detected, and your goals. If you have a relatively long (weeks/months) data collection period and species are rarely detected, you may get better results  by using a longer unit of replication like a week. If your cameras are only open for a week or two and species are encountered very often, 1 day might be better. It also depends a lot on what kind of ecological questions you are asking.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It's quite hard to diagnose this type of error without being able to look at the data and code in detail. However, my first guess would be that the issue is caused by the units of your input data. If you are using meters as the input unit for your distance breaks and transect length (if applicable), and your survey area extends out pretty far (say hundreds of meters) then the default initial value for sigma, which will be relatively small, may not work and the optimization will break as you see here. One easy way to test if this is the case is to change your input units to km. So if your distance breaks were 100m, 200m, 300m they would become 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 km which will be easier for the optimization process to handle. You'd have to change your transect lengths to km as well.

Ken

Indeed, I am working with species that (as a group) are rarely detected well, or in sufficient number. I did start fitting candidate multispecies models using BFGS or L-BFGS-B, but later encountered numerous "non-finite finite-difference value" errors; each one likely due to imprecise parameter estimates (e.g., boundary violations such as p or psi > 1). Additionally, given the sparsity of the data (as well as limited co-occupancy between sites), I was precluded from considering any species-level interactions, unfortunately. Despite there being only 14 sites, each was surveyed 5-6 times per season, for what that's worth.

For the second issue with predicting detection probabilities, I suspect that that problem stems from those issues discussed above, including (1) the lack of species-level interactions in the model, (2) limited species co-occurrences between sites, and (3) imprecise model parameter estimates due to reduced sample size and other related constraints. I was able to identify less-aberrant models in my candidate set (i.e. those still outcompeting the null [intercept-only] model), for which I can generate more precise parameter estimates as well as predictions of occurrence and detection (e.g., marginal, conditional, and co-occupancy and -detection).

Hi Alissa,

The order of the species doesn't matter - if you change the order of the species you will get the same estimates. If the estimate of species1:species2 intercept is positive, then species 1 has greater occupancy probability at sites occupied by species 2. The reverse is also true: species 2 has greater occupancy at sites occupied by species 1. It might be more helpful to think about the value of the parameter it this way: are species 1 and 2 likely to occupy the same sites (species1:species 2 positive), different sites (species1:species2 negative), or be independent of each other (species1:species2 = 0)?

Ken

As it appears your data is in strong violation of the closure assumption (as you've noted), your repeat counts themselves represent different "seasons".

I'm not suggesting you use the Dail-Madsen model (pcountOpen), but it doesn't actually require multiple surveys per period of closure (the version written for unmarked always estimates p, but this estimate is meaningless without repeated surveys, as far as I understand). messages.body_plain:
Hi Joseph,

If you want to understand what is happening when you specify the model
differently in the formula, you should look into model.matrix( ). The
function returns the design matrix of your model and illustrates which
parameters are estimated.

Keep in mind that an interaction term between two variables is just the
product of these two variables. Thus, manually creating an interaction
variable by multiplying two variables (A and B) is equivalent to
including "A:B" in your formula.

##create bogus data for this example
##binary variable
Saline <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 5)
##numeric variable
AvgDepth <- rnorm(n = 10, mean = 20, sd = 1.3)

##model where each group has different intercept and different slopes:
##model parameterized as difference between intercepts vs ref level
##and difference of slopes vs slope of reference level
model.matrix(~ Saline*AvgDepth)
##same as model.matrix(~ Saline + AvgDepth + Saline:AvgDepth)

##model where all groups share common intercept,
##but each group has different slopes:
model.matrix(~ Saline:AvgDepth)

##model where each group has different intercept and different slopes:
##parameterized as intercepts and slopes for each group
model.matrix(~ Saline*Avgdepth-1-Avgdepth)
##compare with model.matrix(~ Saline*AvgDepth) above

As to which model or parameterization is best, it ultimately depends on
the data you have (limitations), the presence of parameters on
boundaries, and your hypotheses.

If this is still unclear, then I suggest you look into textbooks
dealing with classic analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). There is nothing
better than trying examples with lm( ) and rebuilding the estimates
from differences of intercepts or slopes to understand how model
parameterizations work. A quick clue that two parameterizations of your
model are equivalent is when you get identical log-likelihoods for both
models.

Hope it helps,

Marc

Hi Roberta,

I believe you'd just want to use the probability of occupancy (the probability of unoccupied is simply 1 - occupancy).

I neglected to note that you can also extract site-specific (rather than mean) projected occupancy and generate site-specific estimated latent occupancy state.

Site-specific projected occupancy can be obtained using t(projected(model,mean="F")[2,,]). This retrieves the projected occupancy array from your model and transposes it so that rows = sites and columns = seasons.

The posterior distribution of the latent occupancy state is an estimate of true occupancy (which also incorporates information about known occupancy if the species was detected) and can be generated using bup(ranef(model),stat = 'mean') or bup(ranef(model),stat = 'mode') (returning only 1s and 0s). Like the above,  rows = sites and columns = seasons.

- Giancarlo

Hi everyone,

I am using occuMulti for my MSc research. I have datasets for 2 seasons (wet and dry) and want to run multi-species occupancy models with 3 species for each season.

I can run occuMulti for my 3 species for the dry season data with no problems, including the intercept-only model and any combinations of covariates.

When I use the same code for the wet season data, I get NaN errors immediately in the intercept-only model before including any covariates in the detection or occupancy functions. I assume it could be because of sparse data, but the datasets are pretty comparable between the wet and dry seasons, so I don't understand why I'm only getting the error for the wet season.

For the dry season data, there are 97 traps. For the wet season, there are 99 traps (different number due to malfunctioned cams). The 3 species are black-backed jackal, brown hyena, and caracal. The caracal dataset is sparse, 9 detections from 6 sites in the dry season and 14 detections from 13 sites in the wet season.

I have 3 sampling occasions. What I suspect may be throwing the error is the fact that there is only one repeated detection of caracal at the same site for the wet season, while the dry season data has more repeated detections at the same sites.

Hyena has ~40 detections for both seasons and jackal has ~150.

Also, when I try occuMulti on only 2 species at a time, I don't get any errors for the wet season data for any combinations of the 3 species.

Any ideas what could be causing the NaN errors? I'm wondering if there are simply not enough caracal detections to include it in my analysis. occuMulti still gives occupancy estimates, but the NaNs are for the SE, z, and (P > |z|) values.

Thanks for any insight.

> product of these two variables. Thus, manually creating an interaction

>

> ##binary variable

> ##and difference of slopes vs slope of reference level

> ##same as model.matrix(~ Saline + AvgDepth + Saline:AvgDepth)
>
> ##model where all groups share common intercept,
> ##but each group has different slopes:

>

I think you have diagnosed this problem correctly - the sparse caracal dataset is likely causing the issues. This model is pretty data hungry and needs at least some information about detection overlaps for all species. The more interactions you try to estimate the more data are needed and the tougher it  gets. Have you tried fitting the model without attempting to estimate the 3-species interaction (i.e., by setting the formula for the 3-species interaction to '0')? That might at least allow you to include all 3 species in the model and still look at their 2-way interactions. If that doesn't work it's likely you won't be able to include caracal, although you could try fitting the model in a Bayesian framework instead.

I would not avoid using parameter estimates from any model with NaNs like this.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm new to the group, and although I have searched to find an answer to this question, I haven't been able to do so (I apologize if I've overlooked this somewhere).

In short, I have a study with 3 visits to 45 sites (20 in habitat A and 25 in habitat B). I want to compare Prothonotary Warbler density between the two habitats, and adjust for visit-level covariates (observer and wind, for starters). I am using three distance bins: 0-25, 26-50, and 51-100 m.

In trying to build the unmarkedFrameGDS, I am running into issues, particularly associated with yearlySiteCovs. The code below seems to be

y <- PROW.GDISTSAMP[,2:10] # columns 2-10 contain observations in 3 distance intervals from 3 survey periods

breaks <- c(25,50,100)
R <- 45 # survey points
T <- 3 # number of survey visits

# site-level covariates
covs <- data.frame(habitat=PROW.GDISTSAMP[,11]) # Habitat A vs Habitat B

# survey-level covariates: called "yearlySiteCovs" in this R package
wind1 <- PROW.GDISTSAMP[,12]
wind1.f <- as.factor(wind1)
wind2 <- PROW.GDISTSAMP[,13]
wind2.f <- as.factor(wind2)
wind3 <- PROW.GDISTSAMP[,14]
wind3.f <- as.factor(wind3)
wind.df <- data.frame(wind1.f, wind2.f, wind3.f)

surveyor1 <- PROW.GDISTSAMP[,15]
surveyor1.f <- as.factor(surveyor1)
surveyor2 <- PROW.GDISTSAMP[,16]
surveyor2.f <- as.factor(surveyor2)
surveyor3 <- PROW.GDISTSAMP[,17]
surveyor3.f <- as.factor(surveyor3)
surveyor.df <- data.frame(surveyor1.f, surveyor2.f, surveyor3.f)

# Organize data into an Unmarked Data frame for Generalized Distance Sampling
umf <- unmarkedFrameGDS(y=y, siteCovs=covs, yearlySiteCovs=list(Obs=surveyor.df, Wind=wind.df), survey="point", unitsIn="m", dist.breaks=breaks, numPrimary=T)

in viewing "umf" it appears that the survey-level covariates have been duplicated (6 columns for Wind and 6 columns for Observer, whereas there should be three each, i.e., one for each of three site visits).

Thanks for any help or insights in fixing this issue!
Erik

messages.subject_clean: Vacancy for senior statistician at the IATTC
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

two interesting job announcement.

Best regards  --- Marc

https://www.iattc.org/StaffVacancies/_English/IATTC-Senior%20Statistician.pdf

This is a permanent position as a senior statistician, so a good background in both theoretical and applied statistics and related experience is essential for the position. A few medium term projects that the person would work on include

1.       Spatial temporal modelling of skipjack tuna tagging data to deal with spatially limited tagging and the consequent initial non-mixing. This would involve joining a spatio-temporal model of the population distribution with an advection-diffusion model of the tagged individuals. https://www.iattc.org/Meetings/Meetings2021/SAC-12/Docs/_English/SAC-12-06_%20Assessment%20methods%20for%20skipjack%20in%20the%20EPO%20using%20tagging%20data.pdf

2.       Close-kin mark-recapture. This involves using genetics to “tag” adults through kinship (parent offspring pairs and half sibling pairs) and requires developing statistics for the probability of these events and integrating it with the stock assessment model. Experience with statistical analysis of genetic data would be beneficial.  https://www.iattc.org/Meetings/Meetings2021/SAC-12/Docs/_English/SAC-12-14_Considerations%20for%20conducting%20Close%20Kin%20Mark%20Recapture%20of%20stocks%20managed%20by%20IATTC.pdf

3.       Sampling design. The IATTC has substantial observer and port sampling programs, and assists and advises member countries on their sampling programs. The statistical would work on improving, setting up, and analyzing data from several sampling programs.  Experience with sampling programs would be useful.

Our work is also associated with the Center for the Advancement of Population Assessment Methodology (CAPAM)  http://www.capamresearch.org/
